claim: RhoA activates Rac1 via DIA.
source: RhoA activates Rac1 via DIA and inhibits Rac1 via ROCK, while Rac1 inhibits RhoA through PAK.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing DIA knockdown effects on Rac1 activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: RhoA inhibits Rac1 via ROCK.
source: RhoA activates Rac1 via DIA and inhibits Rac1 via ROCK, while Rac1 inhibits RhoA through PAK.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by literature citations and experimental data.

claim: Rac1 inhibits RhoA through PAK.
source: RhoA activates Rac1 via DIA and inhibits Rac1 via ROCK, while Rac1 inhibits RhoA through PAK.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by literature citations describing PAK-mediated inhibition of RhoA-specific GEFs.

claim: In motile, polarized cells, RhoA–ROCK interactions prevail at the rear.
source: Our data suggest that in motile, polarized cells, RhoA–ROCK interactions prevail at the rear, whereas RhoA-DIA interactions dominate at the front where Rac1/Rho oscillations drive protrusions and retractions.
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA data showing higher density of RhoA-ROCK complexes at the cell rear (Figure 1B).

claim: RhoA-DIA interactions dominate at the front where Rac1/Rho oscillations drive protrusions and retractions.
source: Our data suggest that in motile, polarized cells, RhoA–ROCK interactions prevail at the rear, whereas RhoA-DIA interactions dominate at the front where Rac1/Rho oscillations drive protrusions and retractions.
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA data showing higher density of RhoA-DIA complexes at the leading edge (Figure 1A).

claim: At the rear, high RhoA and low Rac1 activities are maintained until a wave of oscillatory GTPase activities from the cell front reaches the rear.
source: At the rear, high RhoA and low Rac1 activities are maintained until a wave of oscillatory GTPase activities from the cell front reaches the rear, inducing transient GTPase oscillations and RhoA activity spikes.
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions and FRET imaging data showing RhoA dynamics (Figure 3).

claim: A wave of oscillatory GTPase activities from the cell front induces transient GTPase oscillations and RhoA activity spikes at the rear.
source: At the rear, high RhoA and low Rac1 activities are maintained until a wave of oscillatory GTPase activities from the cell front reaches the rear, inducing transient GTPase oscillations and RhoA activity spikes.
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions and experimental FRET imaging showing RhoA activity bursts at the rear (Figure 3I, J).

claim: After the rear retracts, the initial GTPase pattern resumes.
source: After the rear retracts, the initial GTPase pattern resumes.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations showing cyclic return to initial state.

claim: Periodic, propagating GTPase waves coordinate distinct GTPase patterns at the leading and trailing edge dynamics in moving cells.
source: Our findings show how periodic, propagating GTPase waves coordinate distinct GTPase patterns at the leading and trailing edge dynamics in moving cells.
evidence: This claim is the main conclusion supported by both modeling and experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cell migration relies on the coordination of actin dynamics at the leading and the trailing edges.
source: Cell migration relies on the coordination of actin dynamics at the leading and the trailing edges (Ridley et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: During mesenchymal migration, protrusive filamentous actin (F-actin) is cyclically polymerized/depolymerized at the cell's leading edge.
source: During the mesenchymal type of migration, protrusive filamentous actin (F-actin) is cyclically polymerized/depolymerized at the cell's leading edge, whereas the contractile, actomyosin-enriched trailing edge forms the rear.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of mesenchymal migration.

claim: The contractile, actomyosin-enriched trailing edge forms the rear during mesenchymal migration.
source: During the mesenchymal type of migration, protrusive filamentous actin (F-actin) is cyclically polymerized/depolymerized at the cell's leading edge, whereas the contractile, actomyosin-enriched trailing edge forms the rear.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of mesenchymal migration.

claim: RhoA and Rac1 control protrusions and retractions at the leading edge as well as the contractility at the rear.
source: Two members of this family, Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) and Ras-related C3 botulinum toxin substrate 1 (Rac1), control protrusions and retractions at the leading edge as well as the contractility at the rear (Felmet et al., 2005; Heasman and Ridley, 2008; Machacek et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: RhoGTPases cycle between an active, GTP-loaded 'on' state and an inactive, GDP-loaded 'off' state.
source: RhoGTPases cycle between an active, GTP-loaded 'on' state and an inactive, GDP-loaded 'off' state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RhoGTPase biochemistry.

claim: Guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) facilitate GDP/GTP exchange thereby activating GTPases.
source: Switches between on and off states are tightly regulated by (i) guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) that facilitate GDP/GTP exchange thereby activating GTPases and (ii) GTPase activating proteins (GAPs) that stimulate GTP hydrolysis and transition to a GDP-bound state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GTPase regulation.

claim: GTPase activating proteins (GAPs) stimulate GTP hydrolysis and transition to a GDP-bound state.
source: Switches between on and off states are tightly regulated by (i) guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) that facilitate GDP/GTP exchange thereby activating GTPases and (ii) GTPase activating proteins (GAPs) that stimulate GTP hydrolysis and transition to a GDP-bound state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GTPase regulation.

claim: Rac1-GTP dominates at the leading edge in polarized cells.
source: A canonic description of mesenchymal cell migration portrays mutually separated zones of Rac1-GTP and RhoA-GTP in polarized cells where Rac1-GTP dominates at the leading edge and RhoA-GTP dominates at the contracted cell rear (Holmes and Edelstein-Keshet, 2016; Holmes et al., 2017; Kunida et al., 2012; Kurokawa and Matsuda, 2005; Pertz et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2013; Zmurchok and Holmes, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations describing the canonical view.

claim: RhoA-GTP dominates at the contracted cell rear in polarized cells.
source: A canonic description of mesenchymal cell migration portrays mutually separated zones of Rac1-GTP and RhoA-GTP in polarized cells where Rac1-GTP dominates at the leading edge and RhoA-GTP dominates at the contracted cell rear (Holmes and Edelstein-Keshet, 2016; Holmes et al., 2017; Kunida et al., 2012; Kurokawa and Matsuda, 2005; Pertz et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2013; Zmurchok and Holmes, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations describing the canonical view.

claim: The distinct distribution of RhoA and Rac1 activities along polarized cells is explained by a mutual antagonism of RhoA and Rac1.
source: This distinct distribution of RhoA and Rac1 activities along polarized cells is explained by a mutual antagonism of RhoA and Rac1 (Edelstein-Keshet et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2008) mediated by downstream effectors of these GTPases (Byrne et al., 2016; Guilluy et al., 2011a; Pertz, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: The Rac1 effector PAK phosphorylates and inhibits multiple RhoA-specific GEFs, including p115-RhoGEF, GEF-H1 and Net1.
source: The Rac1 effector, p21 associated kinase (PAK), phosphorylates and inhibits multiple RhoA-specific GEFs, including p115-RhoGEF, GEF-H1 and Net1 (Alberts et al., 2005; Guilluy et al., 2011a; Rosenfeldt et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Active Rac1 binds and activates p190RhoGAP, which decreases RhoA activity.
source: In addition, active Rac1 binds and activates p190RhoGAP, which decreases RhoA activity (Guilluy et al., 2011a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: RhoA-GTP recruits ROCK, which phosphorylates and activates Rac-specific GAPs, such as FilGAP and ArhGAP22, thereby inhibiting Rac1.
source: In turn, RhoA-GTP recruits the Rho-associated kinase (ROCK), which phosphorylates and activates Rac-specific GAPs, such as FilGAP and ArhGAP22, thereby inhibiting Rac1 (Guilluy et al., 2011a; Ohta et al., 2006; Sanz-Moreno et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Mutual inhibition of RhoA and Rac1 may lead to a bistable behavior where a system can switch between two stable steady states.
source: This mutual inhibition of RhoA and Rac1 may lead to a bistable behavior where a system can switch between two stable steady states, in which GTPase activities alternate between high and low values (Kholodenko, 2006; Mori et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by literature citations and theoretical considerations.

claim: Inhibition of the Rac1 effector PAK maintains both high RhoA and low Rac1 activities and associated morphological changes even after the inhibition is released.
source: The existence of bistable switches is supported by experiments, where inhibition of the Rac1 effector PAK maintains both high RhoA and low Rac1 activities and associated morphological changes even after the inhibition is released (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: At the leading edge of migrating cells, RhoA activation is rapidly followed by Rac1 activation, tracking a protrusion-retraction cycle.
source: At the same time, RhoA and Rac1 do not behave antagonistically at the leading edge of migrating cells. Here, RhoA activation is rapidly followed by Rac1 activation, tracking a protrusion-retraction cycle (Machacek et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Rac1 activation at the leading edge is mediated by the downstream RhoA effector DIA.
source: This Rac1 activation at the leading edge is mediated by the downstream RhoA effector, Diaphanous related formin-1 (DIA), that was shown to localize to the membrane ruffles of motile cells (Tkachenko et al., 2011; Watanabe et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: DIA localizes to the membrane ruffles of motile cells.
source: This Rac1 activation at the leading edge is mediated by the downstream RhoA effector, Diaphanous related formin-1 (DIA), that was shown to localize to the membrane ruffles of motile cells (Tkachenko et al., 2011; Watanabe et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: The RhoA effector ROCK inhibits Rac1 in cell segments other than the leading edge.
source: Thus, in contrast to the RhoA effector ROCK, which inhibits Rac1 in the other cell segments, the RhoA effector DIA can stimulate Rac1 activity at the leading edge.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the contrast with DIA function and supported by literature.

claim: If at the leading edge RhoA activates Rac1 but Rac1 inhibits RhoA, this intertwined network circuitry will force the network to periodically change RhoA and Rac1 activities, giving rise to self-perpetuating oscillations.
source: If at the leading edge RhoA activates Rac1 but Rac1 inhibits RhoA, this intertwined network circuitry of positive and negative loops will force the network to periodically change RhoA and Rac1 activities, giving rise to self-perpetuating oscillations with a constant amplitude and frequency (Kholodenko, 2006; Tsyganov et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical considerations supported by literature citations.

claim: At the trailing edge and cell body, the mutual RhoA and Rac1 inhibition results in the maintenance of a (quasi)steady state with high RhoA activity and low Rac1 activity.
source: By contrast, at the trailing edge and cell body, the mutual RhoA and Rac1 inhibition results in the maintenance of a (quasi)steady state with high RhoA activity and low Rac1 activity.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical considerations and model predictions.

claim: Downregulation of DIA decreased relative activities of both RhoA and Rac1.
source: Downregulation of DIA increased the RhoA abundance and decreased Rac1 abundance, while decreasing relative activities of both RhoA and Rac1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, panels A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decrease of relative Rac1 and RhoA activities induced by DIA knockdown shows that DIA activates Rac1.
source: The decrease of relative Rac1 and RhoA activities induced by DIA knockdown shows that DIA activates Rac1 and also supports the existence of a positive feedback loop between DIA and RhoA described earlier (Kitzing et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by a literature citation.

claim: DIA knockdown supports the existence of a positive feedback loop between DIA and RhoA.
source: The decrease of relative Rac1 and RhoA activities induced by DIA knockdown shows that DIA activates Rac1 and also supports the existence of a positive feedback loop between DIA and RhoA described earlier (Kitzing et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by a literature citation.

claim: The GTPase network features a positive feedback from PAK to Rac1 through several molecular mechanisms.
source: In addition, the GTPase network features another positive feedback from PAK to Rac1 through several molecular mechanisms (Baird et al., 2005; DerMardirossian et al., 2004; Feng et al., 2002; Obermeier et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: The density of the RhoA-DIA complexes is predominantly localized at the cell front and markedly decreased at the rear.
source: The results show that the RhoA-DIA complexes are predominantly localized at the cell front, whereas their density is markedly decreased at the rear (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The density of the RhoA-ROCK complexes increases toward the cell rear and decreases at the leading edge.
source: In contrast, the density of the RhoA-ROCK complexes increases toward the cell rear and decreases at the leading edge (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DIA is mainly localized at the leading edge in polarized cells.
source: These results are in line with protein staining data in polarized cells, which suggest that DIA is mainly localized at the leading edge (Figure 1C), whereas ROCK is abundant at the rear and cell body (Figure 1D; Brandt et al., 2007; Goulimari et al., 2005; Newell-Litwa et al., 2015; Watanabe et al., 1997; Wheeler and Ridley, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1C and literature citations.

claim: ROCK is abundant at the rear and cell body in polarized cells.
source: These results are in line with protein staining data in polarized cells, which suggest that DIA is mainly localized at the leading edge (Figure 1C), whereas ROCK is abundant at the rear and cell body (Figure 1D; Brandt et al., 2007; Goulimari et al., 2005; Newell-Litwa et al., 2015; Watanabe et al., 1997; Wheeler and Ridley, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1D and literature citations.

claim: The RhoA abundance is at least 10-fold larger than the abundance of DIA and ROCK isoforms combined in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: For MDA-MB-231 cells, our quantitative proteomics data showed that the RhoA abundance is at least 10-fold larger than the abundance of DIA and ROCK isoforms combined (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data from a previous study.

claim: The RhoA-effector concentrations depend approximately linearly on the DIA and ROCK abundances.
source: Thus, as shown in the Modeling section of Materials and methods, the RhoA-effector concentrations depend approximately linearly on the DIA and ROCK abundances.
evidence: This claim is derived from mathematical modeling considerations.

claim: The model predicts self-perpetuating oscillations of the RhoA and Rac1 activities at the leading edge.
source: The blue region 1 in Figure 2A corresponds to the self-perpetuating oscillations of the RhoA and Rac1 activities at the leading edge.
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the mathematical model shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A combination of Rac1 activation by RhoA via DIA and RhoA inhibition by Rac1 via PAK results in sustained oscillations of RhoA and Rac1 activities at the leading edge.
source: Thus, a combination of Rac1 activation by RhoA via DIA and RhoA inhibition by Rac1 via PAK (Figure 2B) results in sustained oscillations of RhoA and Rac1 activities at the leading edge (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: Periodic Rac1 activation drives actin polymerization at the leading edge pushing protrusion-retraction cycles.
source: This periodic Rac1 activation drives actin polymerization at the leading edge pushing protrusion-retraction cycles (Machacek et al., 2009; Martin et al., 2016; Pertz, 2010; Tkachenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: The model predicts sustained GTPase oscillations and a stable steady state with high RhoA and low Rac1 activities coexist in area 3 (BiDR regime).
source: The red region 3 corresponds to the coexistence of GTPase oscillations and a stable steady state with high RhoA and low Rac1 activities.
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the mathematical model shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the BiDR region, depending on the initial state, the GTPase network evolves to different dynamic regimes.
source: Depending on the initial state, the GTPase network evolves to different dynamic regimes. If the initial state has high RhoA-GTP and low Rac1-GTP, the GTPase network progresses to a stable steady state, but if the initial state has low RhoA-GTP and high Rac1-GTP, the network will develop sustained oscillations (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the mathematical model shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The model predicts autonomous, repeating cycles of the spatiotemporal GTPase dynamics.
source: The model predicts autonomous, repeating cycles of the spatiotemporal GTPase dynamics (Figure 3D–G and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the spatiotemporal model shown in Figure 3 and Video 1.

claim: For a substantial part of a dynamic cycle, high RhoA-GTP and low Rac1-GTP persist at the cell rear and maintain the rear contraction.
source: For a substantial part of a dynamic cycle, high RhoA-GTP and low Rac1-GTP persist at the cell rear and maintain the rear contraction, whereas active RhoA and Rac1 oscillate at the leading edge, resulting in actin (de)polarization cycles and protrusion-retraction cycles (Figure 3D and F; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the spatiotemporal model shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: Active RhoA and Rac1 oscillate at the leading edge, resulting in actin (de)polarization cycles and protrusion-retraction cycles.
source: For a substantial part of a dynamic cycle, high RhoA-GTP and low Rac1-GTP persist at the cell rear and maintain the rear contraction, whereas active RhoA and Rac1 oscillate at the leading edge, resulting in actin (de)polarization cycles and protrusion-retraction cycles (Figure 3D and F; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the spatiotemporal model shown in Figure 3D and F, supported by a literature citation.

claim: A wave of oscillating Rac1 and RhoA activities slowly propagates from the leading edge toward the cell rear.
source: At the same time, a wave of oscillating Rac1 and RhoA activities slowly propagates from the leading edge toward the cell rear (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the spatiotemporal model shown in Figure 3E and G.

claim: Between the oscillatory RhoA-GTP zone and the areas of high RhoA activity, a zone of low RhoA activity emerges.
source: Between the oscillatory RhoA-GTP zone and the areas of high RhoA activity, a zone of low RhoA activity emerges (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the spatiotemporal model shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The spatiotemporal RhoA activity showed three different zones: oscillations at the leading edge, dark zone of low activity, and light zone of high activity in the cell body and rear.
source: In the initial phase of the cell movement cycle, the spatiotemporal RhoA activity showed three different zones: (i) oscillations at the leading edge, (ii) dark zone of low activity and (iii) light zone of high activity (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel C) in the cell body and rear, matching the model prediction (Figsure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The GTPase activity wave propagated further into the cell, forming zones of high and low RhoA activities.
source: As time progressed, the GTPase activity wave propagated further into the cell (Figure 3I), forming zones of high and low RhoA activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET imaging data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: When the wave of oscillatory GTPase activities reaches the cell rear, it induces several RhoA-GTP spikes.
source: When the wave of oscillatory GTPase activities finally reaches the cell rear, it induces several RhoA-GTP spikes (Figure 3G and I), periods of low RhoA activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panels A-B and D), and subsequent return to the original, high RhoA-GTP at the rear and part of the cell body (Figure 3F and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET imaging data shown in Figure 3G and I.

claim: During a single cellular movement cycle, multiple bursts of RhoA activity appear at the leading edge, whereas at the cell rear, RhoA activity bursts occur only after the RhoA-Rac1 wave has spread through the cell.
source: The model predicts that during a single cellular movement cycle, multiple bursts of RhoA activity appear at the leading edge, whereas at the cell rear, RhoA activity bursts occur only after the RhoA-Rac1 wave has spread through the cell (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the model shown in Video 1.

claim: At the leading edge a burst of RhoA activity happens every minute, while at the cell rear only 1 or 2 bursts happen during 10 min.
source: On average, at the leading edge a burst of RhoA activity happens every minute, while at the cell rear only 1 or 2 bursts happen during 10 min (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Rac1 was mainly active at the leading edge with lower activity in the space between the nucleus and cell rear.
source: Rac1 was mainly active at the leading edge with lower activity in the space between the nucleus and cell rear (Figure 3K), similar to the patterns observed in the model for protrusion-retraction cycles (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Super-resolution images corroborated the Rac1-GTP presence towards the cell nucleus and rear.
source: The GTPase waves can be detected using super-resolution imaging. These images corroborated the Rac1-GTP presence towards the cell nucleus and rear (see super-resolution images in Figure 3L–M and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel E).
evidence: This claim is supported by super-resolution imaging data shown in Figure 3L-M.

claim: PAK inhibition could change the cell shape of MDA-MB-231 cells from mesenchymal to amoeboid.
source: We previously showed that PAK inhibition could change the cell shape of MDA-MB-231 cells from mesenchymal to amoeboid (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The mesenchymal mode of migration features an elongated cell morphology and high Rac1 activity.
source: The mesenchymal mode of migration features an elongated cell morphology and high Rac1 activity, whereas the amoeboid mode is hallmarked by a rounded morphology and high RhoA activity (Sanz-Moreno et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The amoeboid mode of migration is hallmarked by a rounded morphology and high RhoA activity.
source: The mesenchymal mode of migration features an elongated cell morphology and high Rac1 activity, whereas the amoeboid mode is hallmarked by a rounded morphology and high RhoA activity (Sanz-Moreno et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The transition from mesenchymal to amoeboid mode correlated with the hysteresis of active RhoA and Rac1 upon PAK inhibition.
source: Our previous study showed that this transition correlated with the hysteresis of active RhoA and Rac1 upon PAK inhibition (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Hysteresis is the hallmark of bistability.
source: Hysteresis is the hallmark of bistability: if a parameter, such as the PAK abundance, reaches a threshold value, then the system flips from one stable state to another stable state, at which it remains for a prolonged period of time even when this parameter has returned to its initial value (Markevich et al., 2004; Sha et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by literature citations.

claim: A decrease in ROCK activity below a certain threshold results in the formation of several oscillatory centers of GTPase activities featuring high (averaged over time) Rac1 activity.
source: The model predicts that a decrease in ROCK activity below a certain threshold results in the formation of several oscillatory centers of GTPase activities featuring high (averaged over time) Rac1 activity (Video 3).
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the model shown in Video 3.

claim: ROCK inhibition induced multiple Rac1-GTP foci in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: To determine if ROCK inhibition could induce multiple Rac1-GTP foci, we seeded MDA-MB-231 cells on collagen and treated the cells with the pan-ROCK inhibitor Y-27632. After 15 min, we fixed the cells and stained for active Rac1 and F-actin. Spatially resolved Rac1 activity showed two or three Rac1-GTP poles, whereas cells not incubated with the inhibitor were exclusively mono-polar (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, panel A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ROCK inhibition resulted in the existence of several centers of uncoordinated RhoA activities.
source: Using the RhoA-GTP FRET-probe to measure RhoA activity in a spatially resolved manner, Figure 5B showed the existence of several centers of uncoordinated RhoA activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When ROCK is inhibited, a GTPase oscillatory center emerges in the tail with the corresponding increase in the frequency of RhoA-GTP bursts.
source: When ROCK is inhibited, a GTPase oscillatory center emerges in the tail with the corresponding increase in the frequency of RhoA-GTP bursts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, panels B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions and experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ROCK-inhibited cells do not lose polarity but exhibit substantial morphological changes, acquiring largely elongated shapes.
source: As a result, a cell loses the ability to retract the tail. These cells do not lose polarity but exhibit substantial morphological changes, acquiring largely elongated shapes (compare Videos 2 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by video microscopy data shown in Videos 2 and 4.

claim: The total migration distance is smaller for cells treated with ROCK inhibitor than for untreated cells.
source: In line with these results, our experiments suggest that the total migration distance is smaller for cells treated with ROCK inhibitor than for untreated cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, panel D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental migration data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, panel D.

claim: ROCK activity above a certain threshold is necessary for the formation of a single high Rac1 activity center at the leading edge and avoiding the appearance of multiple high Rac1 activity centers in a cell.
source: Summing up, these data suggest that the ROCK activity above a certain threshold is necessary for the formation of a single high Rac1 activity center at the leading edge and avoiding the appearance of multiple high Rac1 activity centers in a cell.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental and modeling results on ROCK inhibition.

claim: ROCK cooperates with PAK to maintain the polarized lamellipodia formation and the cell shape typical for mesenchymal cell movement.
source: Thus, ROCK cooperates with PAK to maintain the polarized lamellipodia formation and the cell shape typical for mesenchymal cell movement.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: RhoGTPases integrate multiple internal and external cues.
source: RhoGTPases are core regulators of mesenchymal and amoeboid cell migration. They integrate multiple internal and external cues (Campa et al., 2015; Devreotes et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2015; Park et al., 2017; Park et al., 2019) and relay information to a variety of cellular protein machineries, including proteins driving actin polymerization and cytoskeleton rearrangements, thereby enabling cell migration (Warner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: RhoGTPases relay information to cellular protein machineries, including proteins driving actin polymerization and cytoskeleton rearrangements, thereby enabling cell migration.
source: They integrate multiple internal and external cues (Campa et al., 2015; Devreotes et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2015; Park et al., 2017; Park et al., 2019) and relay information to a variety of cellular protein machineries, including proteins driving actin polymerization and cytoskeleton rearrangements, thereby enabling cell migration (Warner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The model rationalizes how the amoeboid and mesenchymal types of migration interchange by suppression or over-activation of specific RhoA and Rac1 effectors.
source: Besides, our model rationalizes how the amoeboid and mesenchymal types of migration interchange by suppression or over-activation of specific RhoA and Rac1 effectors.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and experimental validation.

claim: Live cell imaging experiments showed oscillations in RhoA activity at the leading edge.
source: However, live cell imaging experiments showed oscillations in RhoA activity at the leading edge, challenging the traditional view (Machacek et al., 2009; Pertz, 2010; Tkachenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Several studies suggested that RhoA not only inhibits Rac1 via ROCK but also activates Rac1 via DIA.
source: Several studies suggested that RhoA not only inhibits Rac1 via ROCK but also activates Rac1 via DIA (Guilluy et al., 2011a; Tsuji et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Differential localization of DIA and ROCK generates distinct circuitries of RhoA-Rac1 interactions and different RhoA and Rac1 kinetics along a cell.
source: Differential localization of DIA and ROCK, as well as different spatial distribution of GEFs, GAPs, and guanosine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors (de Beco et al., 2018; Nikonova et al., 2013; Tsyganov et al., 2012), generate distinct circuitries of RhoA-Rac1 interactions and different RhoA and Rac1 kinetics along a cell (Figure 2B–F).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data and supported by literature citations.

claim: Oscillations of RhoA and Rac1 activities at the leading edge guide protrusions and retractions.
source: Oscillations of RhoA and Rac1 activities at the leading edge guide protrusions and retractions, whereas high, stable RhoA activity and low Rac1-GTP at the rear maintain focal adhesions and the cell attachment to the substrate.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and established knowledge.

claim: High, stable RhoA activity and low Rac1-GTP at the rear maintain focal adhesions and the cell attachment to the substrate.
source: Oscillations of RhoA and Rac1 activities at the leading edge guide protrusions and retractions, whereas high, stable RhoA activity and low Rac1-GTP at the rear maintain focal adhesions and the cell attachment to the substrate.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and established knowledge.

claim: Periodically repeating RhoGTPase waves connect protrusion-retraction oscillations of RhoA and Rac1 activities at the leading edge and almost stable RhoA and Rac1 activities at the rear.
source: Our model suggests that periodically repeating RhoGTPase waves connect protrusion-retraction oscillations of RhoA and Rac1 activities at the leading edge and almost stable RhoA and Rac1 activities at the rear.
evidence: This claim is a key finding from the model.

claim: The RhoGTPase waves occur due to diffusion fluxes that are induced by different RhoA-GTP and Rac1-GTP concentrations along the cell and the excitable dynamics of RhoA and Rac1 generated by negative and positive feedback loops in the network.
source: The RhoGTPase waves occur due to diffusion fluxes that are induced by different RhoA-GTP and Rac1-GTP concentrations along the cell and the excitable dynamics of RhoA and Rac1 generated by negative and positive feedback loops in the network (Tsyganov et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on model mechanisms supported by a literature citation.

claim: These RhoA and Rac1 activity waves create an autonomous, cyclic mechanism that controls the mesenchymal type of cell migration.
source: These RhoA and Rac1 activity waves create an autonomous, cyclic mechanism that controls the mesenchymal type of cell migration.
evidence: This claim is a key conclusion from the model and experiments.

claim: In the initial phase of cell migration, the Rac1-RhoA oscillations push out and retract lamellopodia at the leading edge permitting the cell to explore its environment and follow chemotactic cues.
source: In the initial phase of cell migration, the Rac1-RhoA oscillations push out and retract lamellopodia at the leading edge permitting the cell to explore its environment and follow chemotactic cues (Machacek et al., 2009), while high RhoA activity at the trailing edge stabilizes cell adhesion (Ren et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and supported by literature citations.

claim: High RhoA activity at the trailing edge stabilizes cell adhesion.
source: In the initial phase of cell migration, the Rac1-RhoA oscillations push out and retract lamellopodia at the leading edge permitting the cell to explore its environment and follow chemotactic cues (Machacek et al., 2009), while high RhoA activity at the trailing edge stabilizes cell adhesion (Ren et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and supported by a literature citation.

claim: In the late migration phase, RhoA activity extends toward the front allowing focal adhesions to form at the front, and stress fibers to generate contractile force in the cell body that will retract the rear.
source: In the late migration phase, RhoA activity extends toward the front allowing focal adhesions to form at the front, and stress fibers to generate contractile force in the cell body that will retract the rear.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: Rac1 activity traveling toward the trailing edge destabilizes focal adhesions at the rear.
source: At the same time, Rac1 activity traveling toward the trailing edge destabilizes focal adhesions at the rear.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: The combination of RhoA and Rac1 activities pulls up the rear resulting in cell movement.
source: The combination of these activities pulls up the rear resulting in cell movement.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: The critical coordination of front and rear dynamics is accomplished by the spatially resolved dynamic regulation of the excitable Rac1 and RhoA system.
source: Their critical coordination is accomplished by the spatially resolved dynamic regulation of the excitable Rac1 and RhoA system described by our mathematical model.
evidence: This claim is a key conclusion from the model.

claim: Crosstalk interactions of the core signaling network with cytoskeleton proteins generate actomyosin waves and the cytoskeletal dynamics required for cell migration.
source: We hypothesize that crosstalk interactions of this core signaling network with cytoskeleton proteins generate actomyosin waves and the cytoskeletal dynamics required for cell migration (Saha et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on model predictions and supported by a literature citation.

claim: Model predictions are supported by imaging and western blot experiments.
source: Model predictions are supported by imaging and western blot experiments.
evidence: This claim summarizes the experimental validation of the model.

claim: Experiments with the RhoA FRET probe corroborated the predictions of RhoA-GTP dynamics at the leading edge and cell body and rear.
source: Experiments with the RhoA FRET probe corroborated the predictions of RhoA-GTP dynamics at the leading edge (Figure 3H) and cell body and rear (Figure 3I and J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET imaging data shown in Figure 3H, I, J.

claim: Cell staining with specific Rac1-GTP antibody provided snapshots of Rac1 activity corresponding to protrusion-retraction cycles and the spreading of Rac1 activity beyond the leading edge into the cell body.
source: Cell staining with specific Rac1-GTP antibody provided snapshots of Rac1 activity corresponding to protrusion-retraction cycles (Figure 3K) and the spreading of Rac1 activity beyond the leading edge into the cell body (Figure 3L and M and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel C, super-resolution microscopy images) as predicted by the model.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3K, L, M.

claim: The model predicted a greater number of RhoA activity bursts at the cell leading edge than at the cell rear during a cycle of periodic wave propagation, which is fully supported by experimental data.
source: During a cycle of periodic wave propagation, the model has predicted a greater number of RhoA activity bursts at the cell leading edge than at the cell rear, which is fully supported by our data (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Western blot experiments showed the hysteresis of RhoA and Rac1 activities following PAK inhibition and then washing-out the inhibitor.
source: Our previous western blot experiments showed the hysteresis of RhoA and Rac1 activities following PAK inhibition and then washing-out the inhibitor (Byrne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The reaction-diffusion model demonstrates the hysteresis of the averaged RhoGTPase activities for the non-stationary spatiotemporal dynamics.
source: A reaction-diffusion model of the RhoGTPase dynamics developed here demonstrates the hysteresis of the averaged RhoGTPase activities for the non-stationary spatiotemporal dynamics, – a novel phenomenon previously observed in biology for switches between steady states of bistable systems (Bagowski and Ferrell, 2001; Bhalla et al., 2002; Craciun et al., 2006; Delbrück, 1949; Ferrell, 2002; Monod and Jacob, 1961; Xiong and Ferrell, 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and supported by literature citations.

claim: DIA downregulation by siRNA resulted in an increase in RhoA abundance and a decrease in Rac1 abundance.
source: At the same time, DIA downregulation by siRNA resulted in substantial rewiring of the RhoA-Rac1 signaling network, manifested by an increase in RhoA abundance and a decrease in Rac1 abundance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, panels A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Model simulations show that changes in RhoA and Rac1 abundance following DIA downregulation can decrease a threshold DIA abundance required to maintain the initial GTPase dynamics in time and space.
source: Model simulations show that these changes can decrease a threshold DIA abundance required to maintain the initial GTPase dynamics in time and space (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, panel E).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, panel E.

claim: Cells tend to adapt to DIA1 perturbation by adjusting other protein abundances to keep a minimally perturbed Rho-Rac signaling pattern.
source: Thus, cells tend to adapt to DIA1 perturbation by adjusting other protein abundances to keep a minimally perturbed Rho-Rac signaling pattern.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The periodic waves of Rac1-RhoA activities propagate through the entire cell, coordinating protrusion-retraction cycles at the front and the adhesion-retraction cycle at the rear.
source: The periodic waves of Rac1-RhoA activities described in this paper propagate through the entire cell, coordinating protrusion-retraction cycles at the front and the adhesion-retraction cycle at the rear, and are different from travelling waves reported previously.
evidence: This claim is a key finding distinguishing this work from previous studies.

claim: The periodic waves of Rac1-RhoA activities are different from trigger protein phosphorylation waves that propagate in spatially distributed bistable signaling cascades.
source: These waves also differ from trigger protein phosphorylation waves that propagate in spatially distributed bistable signaling cascades (Kholodenko, 2009; Markevich et al., 2006; Muñoz-García et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim distinguishes the waves described in this work from other types of signaling waves, supported by literature citations.

claim: Wave interactions with deforming cell boundaries will likely modulate the propagation patterns.
source: Another aspect of migration is that cells continuously change shapes during their movement. Wave interactions with deforming cell boundaries will likely modulate the propagation patterns (Cao et al., 2019), which can be further analyzed in a future research.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about future research directions supported by a literature citation.

claim: Microtubules can play an important role in the spatial localization of RhoGTPase related proteins and the coordination of front and back signaling.
source: It was suggested that microtubules can play an important role in the spatial localization of RhoGTPase related proteins and the coordination of front and back signaling (Cullis et al., 2014; Meiri et al., 2012; Ren et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Staining intensities of F-actin at the front and pMLC2 at the rear showed that these intensities were neither positively correlated nor anticorrelated in polarized neutrophils.
source: Staining intensities of F-actin, an indicator of Rac signaling, at the front of polarized neutrophils and phosphorylated myosin light chain 2 (pMLC2), an indicator of RhoA signaling, at the cell rear showed that these intensities were neither positively correlated nor anticorrelated (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The buffering of the front and rear signaling was completely destroyed by the disruption of microtubules.
source: This discovered buffering of the front and rear signaling was completely destroyed by the disruption of microtubules (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Different spatial concentration profiles of RhoA and Rac1 downstream effectors might depend on the microtubule network.
source: Different spatial concentration profiles of RhoA and Rac1 downstream effectors considered in our model might depend on the microtubule network.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the model and literature.

claim: Mechanical tension and mechano-chemical feedback have been suggested as mechanisms coordinating behaviors at the cell front and the rear.
source: Mechanical tension and mechano-chemical feedback have also been suggested as mechanisms coordinating behaviors at the cell front and the rear (Abu Shah and Keren, 2013; Bays et al., 2014; Collins et al., 2012; Guilluy et al., 2011b; Lessey et al., 2012; Park et al., 2017; Saha et al., 2018; Warner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Membrane tension is responsible for maintaining front-back polarity rather than diffusible molecules generated at the cell leading edge.
source: It was proposed that membrane tension is responsible for maintaining front-back polarity rather than diffusible molecules generated at the cell leading edge (Houk et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Membrane tension propagates only locally and fails to mediate long-range signaling.
source: However, subsequent work, which exploited a fluid dynamic model with the flow resistance emerging from cytoskeleton-bound transmembrane proteins, showed that membrane tension propagates only locally and fails to mediate long-range signaling (Shi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Mechanics only modulates biochemical signaling.
source: These findings support a view that mechanics only modulates biochemical signaling, as suggested by our model.
evidence: This claim is inferred from literature findings and the model.

claim: The spatiotemporal model of RhoA-Rac1 signaling represents a minimal, experimentally validated model of the biochemical RhoGTPase network that regulates cell migration.
source: In summary, our spatiotemporal model of RhoA-Rac1 signaling proposes how different GTPase dynamics at the cell front and rear are coupled and explains the changes in signaling patterns and cell shapes upon inhibition of GTPase effectors. It represents a minimal, experimentally validated model of the biochemical RhoGTPase network that regulates cell migration.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main contribution of the work.

claim: This core biochemical network might be a foundation of detailed mechanistic models that would include many more signaling and cytoskeleton proteins.
source: This core biochemical network might be a foundation of detailed mechanistic models that would include many more signaling and cytoskeleton proteins, such as key RhoGEFs and RhoGAPs out of 145 known proteins.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about future model development.
